newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Metals - Copper price seen firm on tight scrap.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Copper price seen firm on tight scrap.

text.p: Far East metals traders, settling in for a quiet week as China celebrates the 47th anniversary of its communist revolution, said tighter copper scrap supply is the only factor supporting world copper prices.
"Scrap is getting tight, it's almost impossible to get hold of," a Singapore trader said on Monday.
Scrap with 94 percent copper content was now costing the same as cathode, the manager of a refinery near Shanghai said.
"Right now, you must pay 83 (U.S.) cents a pound, which means $1,829 per tonne of 94 percent copper scrap," he said.
Late last week, dealers in the United States were quoting a nominal 75 U.S. cents per pound for No.2 scrap copper.
With additional taxes and charges, the price of a tonne of scrap in China was $1,950, the refinery manager said, equal to the cost of a tonne of cathode before refining costs kicked in.
"It doesn't work, so we have to look for replacement for 94 percent," he said.

"We would be able to run our refinery on the basis of current contracts to the end of November. So there is two months supply guaranteed. We have to find supplies for after that and this is what we must do every day now," he said.

Blister was not considered a viable replacement, trade sources in China and elsewhere in the region said, because it contained gold and silver that had to be extracted and then sold to the Chinese central bank at lower than world prices.
But even so the discount for blister against cathode had shortened from $300-$330 a tonne to just $95, sources said.
"This is not because people are holding back from offering, it is because there is not enough material," a trader said.
Raw material shortages could start to pinch refineries if they were unable to find replacement for scrap, though many had already become accustomed to living hand-to-mouth, he said.
"China might have enough concentrate but the overall increase in smelter capacity doesn't cover the shortage of refining capacity and the raw material shortage," another Hong Kong source said.
Latest customs figures show China's imports of uncast and raw copper rose 24 percent year-on-year to 401,080 tonnes in the first eight months of 1996.
The state press reported falling domestic prices were to blame for the heavy imports and said they were unlikely to rebound before the end of 1996.
The domestic Chinese price of copper fell steadily in the first seven months of 1996 to around 23,000 yuan ($2,771) per tonne by July, from 25,700 yuan early in the year, it said.
The closing price on the Shanghai Metal Exchange on Friday for the most active January contract was 20,160 yuan.
The State Statisical Bureau reported in mid-September that copper output hit 591,00 tonnes in the first eight months, up 7.22 percent compared with the same period of 1995.
China's National Day holiday has closed exchanges, banks and most businesses until Wednesday, though trade and industry sources did not expect the market to pick up until next week.
Premiums on base metals deliveries remained unchanged.
Copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) nudged three-week peaks on Friday, though highs near $1,990 a tonne proved too tempting and triggered profit-taking -- said to include Chinese.
Last business was at $1,957 a tonne, even with slide-backs still up $13 from the kerb close on Thursday.
One source in Singapore said on Monday the tightness of scrap was the only fundamental factor bouying the copper price.
